claim: RNA editing by adenosine deamination alters genetic information from the genomic blueprint.
source: RNA editing by adenosine deamination alters genetic information from the genomic blueprint.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about RNA editing that is supported by established scientific knowledge and is cited in the introduction.

claim: When RNA editing recodes mRNAs, it gives organisms the option to express diverse, functionally distinct, protein isoforms.
source: When it recodes mRNAs, it gives organisms the option to express diverse, functionally distinct, protein isoforms.
evidence: This statement is based on established understanding of the functional consequences of RNA editing.

claim: All eumetazoans, from cnidarians to humans, express RNA editing enzymes.
source: All eumetazoans, from cnidarians to humans, express RNA editing enzymes.
evidence: This is a broad statement about the phylogenetic distribution of RNA editing enzymes, supported by scientific literature.

claim: Transcriptome-wide screens have only uncovered about 25 transcripts harboring conserved recoding RNA editing sites in mammals.
source: However, transcriptome-wide screens have only uncovered about 25 transcripts harboring conserved recoding RNA editing sites in mammals and several hundred recoding sites in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior studies on RNA editing in mammals.

claim: Transcriptome-wide screens have uncovered several hundred recoding sites in Drosophila.
source: However, transcriptome-wide screens have only uncovered about 25 transcripts harboring conserved recoding RNA editing sites in mammals and several hundred recoding sites in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior studies on RNA editing in Drosophila.

claim: The squid Doryteuthis pealeii recodes proteins by RNA editing to an unprecedented extent.
source: Here we employ a novel bioinformatic approach with extensive validation to show that the squid Doryteuthis pealeii recodes proteins by RNA editing to an unprecedented extent.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: 57,108 recoding sites were identified in the squid nervous system.
source: We identify 57,108 recoding sites in the nervous system, affecting the majority of the proteins studied.
evidence: This specific number is derived from the bioinformatic analysis of sequencing data.

claim: RNA editing in squid affects the majority of the proteins studied.
source: We identify 57,108 recoding sites in the nervous system, affecting the majority of the proteins studied.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that editing sites were found in a large proportion of identified ORFs.

claim: Recoding by RNA editing in squid is tissue-dependent.
source: Recoding is tissue-dependent, and enriched in genes with neuronal and cytoskeletal functions, suggesting it plays an important role in brain physiology.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis showing different editing levels across tissues.

claim: Recoding by RNA editing in squid is enriched in genes with neuronal and cytoskeletal functions.
source: Recoding is tissue-dependent, and enriched in genes with neuronal and cytoskeletal functions, suggesting it plays an important role in brain physiology.
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis and KEGG pathway mapping.

claim: RNA editing plays an important role in brain physiology in squid.
source: Recoding is tissue-dependent, and enriched in genes with neuronal and cytoskeletal functions, suggesting it plays an important role in brain physiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of editing in neuronal genes and the tissue-specific patterns observed.

claim: Inosine is interpreted as guanosine by the cellular machinery.
source: Because inosine is interpreted as guanosine by the cellular machinery, this process can recode codons (Basilio et al., 1962).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in molecular biology, supported by the cited reference.

claim: A-to-I RNA editing is catalyzed by the ADAR family of enzymes.
source: A-to-I RNA editing is catalyzed by the ADAR (adenosine deaminase that acts on RNA) family of enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic mechanism of A-to-I editing.

claim: All eumetazoans, from cnidarians to mammals, express ADARs.
source: All eumetazoans, from cnidarians to mammals, express ADARs but the extent to which they use them to recode has been explored in few representatives (Nishikura, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic studies cited in the reference.

claim: The extent to which organisms use ADARs to recode has been explored in few representatives.
source: All eumetazoans, from cnidarians to mammals, express ADARs but the extent to which they use them to recode has been explored in few representatives (Nishikura, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the limited scope of prior research, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Transcriptome-wide screens for RNA editing have been limited to organisms with a sequenced genome.
source: So far, such studies have been limited to organisms with a sequenced genome (Ramaswami et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references describing prior methodologies.

claim: In humans, inosine is abundant in RNA.
source: In humans, inosine is abundant in RNA (Paul and Bass, 1998; Bazak et al., 2014), but almost all of it lies within transcribed repetitive elements in untranslated regions or introns (Nishikura, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references on human RNA editing.

claim: Almost all inosine in human RNA lies within transcribed repetitive elements in untranslated regions or introns.
source: In humans, inosine is abundant in RNA (Paul and Bass, 1998; Bazak et al., 2014), but almost all of it lies within transcribed repetitive elements in untranslated regions or introns (Nishikura, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference on the distribution of editing sites in humans.

claim: A compilation of recoding sites in human transcriptomes revealed 1183 events.
source: A compilation of recoding sites in human transcriptomes revealed 1183 events (Xu and Zhang, 2014), but most were observed in only a single sample.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Most recoding events in human transcriptomes were observed in only a single sample.
source: A compilation of recoding sites in human transcriptomes revealed 1183 events (Xu and Zhang, 2014), but most were observed in only a single sample.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Individual searches uncovered only 115 non-repetitive recoding events in humans.
source: Individual searches (Danecek et al., 2012; Ramaswami et al., 2013) uncovered only 115 (non-repetitive) recoding events, and 53 in mice; 34 recoding sites are conserved across mammals (Pinto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Individual searches uncovered 53 recoding events in mice.
source: Individual searches (Danecek et al., 2012; Ramaswami et al., 2013) uncovered only 115 (non-repetitive) recoding events, and 53 in mice; 34 recoding sites are conserved across mammals (Pinto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: 34 recoding sites are conserved across mammals.
source: Individual searches (Danecek et al., 2012; Ramaswami et al., 2013) uncovered only 115 (non-repetitive) recoding events, and 53 in mice; 34 recoding sites are conserved across mammals (Pinto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: In Drosophila, an order of magnitude more recoding sites have been identified compared to mammals.
source: In Drosophila, an order of magnitude more recoding sites have been identified, residing in about 3% of all messages (St Laurent et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Recoding sites in Drosophila reside in about 3% of all messages.
source: In Drosophila, an order of magnitude more recoding sites have been identified, residing in about 3% of all messages (St Laurent et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Scores of recoding sites have been uncovered in a small number of squid and octopus transcripts encoding potassium channels, ADARs, and ion pumps using traditional cloning methods.
source: For example, using traditional cloning methods, scores of recoding sites have been uncovered in a small number of squid and octopus transcripts encoding potassium channels, ADARs, and ion pumps (Garrett and Rosenthal, 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: There are no genomes available for cephalopods.
source: As for most organisms, there are no genomes available for cephalopods.
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of genomic resources at the time of the study.

claim: Almost 60% of all mRNAs studied in squid harbor recoding events.
source: Surprisingly, almost 60% of all mRNAs studied harbor recoding events, and most at multiple sites.
evidence: This is derived from the data showing 6991 out of 12,039 ORFs contain recoding sites.

claim: Most squid mRNAs with recoding events harbor multiple sites.
source: Surprisingly, almost 60% of all mRNAs studied harbor recoding events, and most at multiple sites.
evidence: This is supported by the distribution data showing many proteins with multiple editing sites.

claim: Squid shows orders of magnitude more recoding in the proteome than any other species studied to date.
source: These data show orders of magnitude more recoding in the squid proteome than in any other species studied to date.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: In squid, editing is so pervasive that the central dogma should be modified to include this process.
source: In squid, editing is so pervasive that the central dogma should be modified to include this process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the extensive editing observed in squid.

claim: Extensive recoding may be common in many organisms, rivaling alternative splicing as a means of creating functional diversity.
source: Our results open the possibility that extensive recoding is common in many organisms, rivaling alternative splicing as a means of creating functional diversity.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the squid findings.

claim: The study generated millions of RNA and genomic DNA reads from an individual squid.
source: To detect RNA editing sites in the squid nervous system, we generated millions of RNA and genomic DNA reads from an individual squid.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The method used a de novo transcriptome as the point of reference instead of a genome.
source: Our method differed from previous approaches by using a de novo transcriptome as the point of reference instead of a genome (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the novel methodological approach, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: If the majority of RNA reads were edited ('strong' editing sites), the transcriptome would differ from the genomic DNA and read 'G' where gDNA reads would show 'A'.
source: If the majority of RNA reads were edited ('strong' editing sites), the transcriptome would differ from the genomic DNA and read 'G' where gDNA reads would show 'A' (the sequencing process identifies inosines as guanosines).
evidence: This explains the logic behind the detection method for strong editing sites.

claim: The sequencing process identifies inosines as guanosines.
source: If the majority of RNA reads were edited ('strong' editing sites), the transcriptome would differ from the genomic DNA and read 'G' where gDNA reads would show 'A' (the sequencing process identifies inosines as guanosines).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sequencing technology.

claim: At positions where editing occurred in the minority of RNA-seq reads ('weak' editing sites), the transcriptome and the genomic DNA would be identical.
source: At positions where editing occurred in the minority of RNA-seq reads ('weak' editing sites), however, the transcriptome and the genomic DNA would be identical.
evidence: This explains the logic behind the detection method for weak editing sites.

claim: Weak editing sites were detected by identifying variability in RNA-seq, but not DNA-seq, reads.
source: These sites were detected by identifying variability in RNA-seq, but not DNA-seq, reads (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the detection method, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The general approach is applicable to all organisms that lack a sequenced genome.
source: This general approach is applicable to all organisms that lack a sequenced genome.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applicability of the method.

claim: cDNA was sequenced from the giant axon system (giant fiber lobe: GFL) and the optic lobes (OL).
source: We sequenced cDNA from the giant axon system (giant fiber lobe: GFL), the optic lobes (OL) and matching germline gDNA isolated from the same animal.
evidence: This describes the experimental samples used.

claim: Matching germline gDNA was isolated from the same animal as the GFL and OL samples.
source: We sequenced cDNA from the giant axon system (giant fiber lobe: GFL), the optic lobes (OL) and matching germline gDNA isolated from the same animal.
evidence: This describes the experimental samples used.

claim: cDNA was also sequenced from the vertical lobe (VL), buccal ganglion (BG) and the Stellate Ganglion (SG) from another animal.
source: cDNA was also sequenced from the vertical lobe (VL), buccal ganglion (BG) and the Stellate Ganglion (SG) from another animal (The SG and GFL are parts of the peripheral nervous system; all the rest are from the central nervous system).
evidence: This describes additional experimental samples used.

claim: The SG and GFL are parts of the peripheral nervous system.
source: cDNA was also sequenced from the vertical lobe (VL), buccal ganglion (BG) and the Stellate Ganglion (SG) from another animal (The SG and GFL are parts of the peripheral nervous system; all the rest are from the central nervous system).
evidence: This is anatomical information about the tissue samples.

claim: The VL, BG, and OL are from the central nervous system.
source: cDNA was also sequenced from the vertical lobe (VL), buccal ganglion (BG) and the Stellate Ganglion (SG) from another animal (The SG and GFL are parts of the peripheral nervous system; all the rest are from the central nervous system).
evidence: This is anatomical information about the tissue samples.

claim: The pipeline identified 81,930 weak sites due to A-to-G transitions.
source: Surprisingly, our pipeline identified 81,930 weak sites, and 5644 strong sites, due to A-to-G transitions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a specific result from the bioinformatic analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pipeline identified 5644 strong sites due to A-to-G transitions.
source: Surprisingly, our pipeline identified 81,930 weak sites, and 5644 strong sites, due to A-to-G transitions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a specific result from the bioinformatic analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only 12,403 weak sites were identified for the other 11 possible types of modifications.
source: Only 12,403 weak sites and 219 strong sites were identified for the other 11 possible types of modifications.
evidence: This is a specific result from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Only 219 strong sites were identified for the other 11 possible types of modifications.
source: Only 12,403 weak sites and 219 strong sites were identified for the other 11 possible types of modifications.
evidence: This is a specific result from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The false-positive rate for weak sites is 15%.
source: These numbers suggest false-positive rates of 15% and 4% respectively, mainly due to transcriptome assembly problems, SNPs, somatic mutations and systematic mis-alignments.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the ratio of A-to-G to non-A-to-G modifications.

claim: The false-positive rate for strong sites is 4%.
source: These numbers suggest false-positive rates of 15% and 4% respectively, mainly due to transcriptome assembly problems, SNPs, somatic mutations and systematic mis-alignments.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the ratio of A-to-G to non-A-to-G modifications.

claim: False-positives are mainly due to transcriptome assembly problems, SNPs, somatic mutations and systematic mis-alignments.
source: These numbers suggest false-positive rates of 15% and 4% respectively, mainly due to transcriptome assembly problems, SNPs, somatic mutations and systematic mis-alignments.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of false-positive signals.

claim: The false-positive rates in squid are considerably lower than those for similar searches for editing within human coding sequences where a genome reference was employed.
source: Note that these false-positive rates are considerably lower than those for similar searches for editing within human coding sequences, where a genome reference was employed (Ramaswami et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior studies, supported by the cited reference.

claim: The pipeline was applied to similarly sized data sets from a human blood sample and from the rhesus macaque brain.
source: First, we applied our pipeline to similarly sized data sets from a human blood sample and from the rhesus macaque brain, each containing matching RNA and DNA sequence reads.
evidence: This describes a control experiment to validate the method.

claim: In human and rhesus macaque samples, the quantity of AG mismatches in coding regions were similar to those from non-AG mismatches.
source: As expected for mammals, the quantity of AG mismatches in coding regions were similar to those from non-AG mismatches, and both were quantitatively indistinguishable from the noise determined from the squid data (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The enormous number of AG mismatches in the squid data is not an artefact of the analysis pipeline.
source: These controls demonstrate that the enormous number of AG mismatches in the squid data is not an artefact of our analysis pipeline.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments.

claim: A-to-I editing sites in squid tend to cluster.
source: Similar to A-to-I editing sites in other organisms (Morse et al., 2002; Levanon et al., 2004; Kleinberger and Eisenberg, 2010), those identified here tend to cluster and show distinctive 5′ and 3′ neighbor preferences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and comparison with other organisms.

claim: A-to-I editing sites in squid show distinctive 5′ and 3′ neighbor preferences.
source: Similar to A-to-I editing sites in other organisms (Morse et al., 2002; Levanon et al., 2004; Kleinberger and Eisenberg, 2010), those identified here tend to cluster and show distinctive 5′ and 3′ neighbor preferences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and comparison with other organisms.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of results from five tissues reveals that A-to-G modifications exhibit clear tissue-specificity.
source: In addition, hierarchical clustering of results from five tissues reveals that A-to-G modifications, but not other types, exhibit clear tissue-specificity, suggesting they do not result from genomic polymorphisms and mapping artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Non A-to-G modifications do not exhibit clear tissue-specificity.
source: In addition, hierarchical clustering of results from five tissues reveals that A-to-G modifications, but not other types, exhibit clear tissue-specificity, suggesting they do not result from genomic polymorphisms and mapping artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The tissue-specificity of A-to-G modifications suggests they do not result from genomic polymorphisms and mapping artifacts.
source: In addition, hierarchical clustering of results from five tissues reveals that A-to-G modifications, but not other types, exhibit clear tissue-specificity, suggesting they do not result from genomic polymorphisms and mapping artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tissue-specificity pattern.

claim: No A-to-G overrepresentation is observed in mitochondria-encoded genes.
source: No A-to-G overrepresentation is observed in mitochondria-encoded genes (Figure 2A), in agreement with the absence of ADARs, and by extension A-to-I editing, in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with the known absence of ADARs in mitochondria.

claim: ADARs are absent in the mitochondria.
source: No A-to-G overrepresentation is observed in mitochondria-encoded genes (Figure 2A), in agreement with the absence of ADARs, and by extension A-to-I editing, in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADAR localization.

claim: A-to-I editing is absent in the mitochondria.
source: No A-to-G overrepresentation is observed in mitochondria-encoded genes (Figure 2A), in agreement with the absence of ADARs, and by extension A-to-I editing, in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of ADARs in mitochondria.

claim: Direct Sanger sequencing from a second individual confirmed editing at 40/40 A-to-G sites.
source: Finally, direct Sanger sequencing from a second individual confirmed editing at 40/40 A-to-G sites, and deep-sequencing validated 120/143 A-to-G sites but none of the 12 non A-to-G sites tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1C–G).
evidence: This is a validation result using Sanger sequencing.

claim: Deep-sequencing validated 120/143 A-to-G sites.
source: Finally, direct Sanger sequencing from a second individual confirmed editing at 40/40 A-to-G sites, and deep-sequencing validated 120/143 A-to-G sites but none of the 12 non A-to-G sites tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1C–G).
evidence: This is a validation result using deep sequencing.

claim: Deep-sequencing validated none of the 12 non A-to-G sites tested.
source: Finally, direct Sanger sequencing from a second individual confirmed editing at 40/40 A-to-G sites, and deep-sequencing validated 120/143 A-to-G sites but none of the 12 non A-to-G sites tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1C–G).
evidence: This is a validation result using deep sequencing.

claim: The majority of the A-to-G modifications are true editing events.
source: Taken together, the overrepresentation of A-to-G modifications over all other types, the motifs surrounding the A-to-G sites, the tissue-specific modification levels, and the validation experiments, provide evidence that the majority of the A-to-G modifications are true editing events, while most non A-to-G modifications are likely technical artifacts or genomic variations (Zaranek et al., 2010; Ramaswami et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Most non A-to-G modifications are likely technical artifacts or genomic variations.
source: Taken together, the overrepresentation of A-to-G modifications over all other types, the motifs surrounding the A-to-G sites, the tissue-specific modification levels, and the validation experiments, provide evidence that the majority of the A-to-G modifications are true editing events, while most non A-to-G modifications are likely technical artifacts or genomic variations (Zaranek et al., 2010; Ramaswami et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence and supported by cited references.

claim: Overall, 57,108 recoding events were detected in 6991/12,039 ORFs.
source: Unlike with humans, the large number of A-to-I editing events translates into a large number of recoding events: Overall, 57,108 recoding events were detected in 6991/12,039 ORFs.
evidence: This is a specific result from the analysis.

claim: The numbers of recoding events in squid are orders of magnitude higher than any other species studied.
source: These numbers are orders of magnitude higher than any other species studied (Danecek et al., 2012; Ramaswami et al., 2013; St Laurent et al., 2013; Pinto et al., 2014) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a comparison with other species, shown in Figure 2B and supported by cited references.

claim: About 1/3 of squid proteins harbor ≥3 recoding sites.
source: Moreover, a large fraction of the proteins are recoded at multiple sites (Figure 3A): about 1/3 harbor ≥3 sites and 10% harbor ≥10 sites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 10% of squid proteins harbor ≥10 recoding sites.
source: Moreover, a large fraction of the proteins are recoded at multiple sites (Figure 3A): about 1/3 harbor ≥3 sites and 10% harbor ≥10 sites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: About 10% of the squid proteins harbor ≥5 sites with editing levels >10%.
source: Even when focusing only on recoding sites with editing levels >10%, about 10% of the squid proteins harbor ≥5 sites (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ORF encoding α Spectrin has 247 recoding sites.
source: On the extreme end of the spectrum, the ORFs encoding α Spectrin and Piccolo have 247 and 182 recoding sites, respectively (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specific result shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ORF encoding Piccolo has 182 recoding sites.
source: On the extreme end of the spectrum, the ORFs encoding α Spectrin and Piccolo have 247 and 182 recoding sites, respectively (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specific result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only annotated ORFs were examined in the pipeline.
source: It should be noted that only annotated ORFs were examined in our pipeline, and the number of editing sites did not saturate with respect to the number of sequence reads (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of the analysis.

claim: The number of editing sites did not saturate with respect to the number of sequence reads.
source: It should be noted that only annotated ORFs were examined in our pipeline, and the number of editing sites did not saturate with respect to the number of sequence reads (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Incompleteness of the de novo transcriptome may cause the pipeline to miss many additional sites.
source: Moreover, incompleteness of the de novo transcriptome, as well as incorrect assembly of paralogs and splice variants, may cause our pipeline to miss many additional sites (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of the method.

claim: Incorrect assembly of paralogs and splice variants may cause the pipeline to miss many additional sites.
source: Moreover, incompleteness of the de novo transcriptome, as well as incorrect assembly of paralogs and splice variants, may cause our pipeline to miss many additional sites (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of the method.

claim: There are probably many more recoding sites in the squid transcriptome than reported.
source: Therefore there are probably many more recoding sites in the squid transcriptome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-saturation of detection and methodological limitations.

claim: Recoding events are enriched in genes with neuronal and cytoskeletal functions.
source: Consistent with other organisms (Stapleton et al., 2006), recoding events are enriched in genes with neuronal and cytoskeletal functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: This is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and comparison with other organisms.

claim: Of the 27 proteins in the 'Synaptic vesicle cycle' pathway, 22 are edited.
source: For example, of the 27 proteins in the 'Synaptic vesicle cycle' pathway, 22 are edited and 14 heavily so (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Of the 27 proteins in the 'Synaptic vesicle cycle' pathway, 14 are heavily edited.
source: For example, of the 27 proteins in the 'Synaptic vesicle cycle' pathway, 22 are edited and 14 heavily so (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Of the 39 proteins in the 'Axon guidance' pathway, 33 are edited.
source: Similarly, of the 39 proteins in the 'Axon guidance' pathway, 33 are edited and 19 heavily so.
evidence: This is a result from KEGG pathway analysis.

claim: Of the 39 proteins in the 'Axon guidance' pathway, 19 are heavily edited.
source: Similarly, of the 39 proteins in the 'Axon guidance' pathway, 33 are edited and 19 heavily so.
evidence: This is a result from KEGG pathway analysis.

claim: Proteins in the pathways 'Ribosome' and 'RNA polymerase' are edited less than average.
source: By contrast, proteins in the pathways 'Ribosome' and 'RNA polymerase' are edited less than average (Supplementary file 1I), demonstrating that some pathways may be protected from editing.
evidence: This is a result from KEGG pathway analysis.

claim: Some pathways may be protected from editing.
source: By contrast, proteins in the pathways 'Ribosome' and 'RNA polymerase' are edited less than average (Supplementary file 1I), demonstrating that some pathways may be protected from editing.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that certain pathways have lower editing rates.

claim: Editing levels observed in non-nervous system tissues are considerably lower.
source: Consistently, editing levels observed in non-nervous system tissues are considerably lower (Alon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data from non-neuronal tissues.

claim: For sites with high editing levels in squid, the fraction of nonsynonymous events is higher than expected by chance.
source: Strikingly, for sites with high editing levels in squid, the opposite is true (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, contrasting with the situation in humans.

claim: Recoding events favor creation of glycine and arginine, mainly at the expense of lysine.
source: Recoding events favor creation of glycine and arginine, mainly at the expense of lysine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Highly edited sites within conserved domains tend to recode to amino acids that occur frequently in other species at the same position.
source: Moreover, highly edited sites within conserved domains tend to recode to amino acids that occur frequently in other species at the same position (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting selection towards functional substitutions and against deleterious ones.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pattern of amino acid substitutions suggests selection towards functional substitutions and against deleterious ones.
source: Moreover, highly edited sites within conserved domains tend to recode to amino acids that occur frequently in other species at the same position (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting selection towards functional substitutions and against deleterious ones.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that highly edited sites create amino acids found in conserved domains.

claim: 87 GFL ORFs that encode voltage and neurotransmitter gated ion channels, ion transporters, synaptic release machinery and molecular motors were identified.
source: In total, 87 GFL ORFs that encode voltage and neurotransmitter gated ion channels, ion transporters, synaptic release machinery and molecular motors were identified in our transcriptome.
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: 70% of the 87 GFL ORFs encoding ion channels, transporters, and synaptic machinery harbored editing sites.
source: In agreement with the overall editing frequency in squid, 70% harbored editing sites.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of specific functional categories.

claim: 54% of the 87 GFL ORFs encoding ion channels, transporters, and synaptic machinery were heavily edited.
source: Unexpectedly, however, 54% were heavily edited, many more than the 24% expected.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of specific functional categories.

claim: The 54% heavily edited rate is many more than the 24% expected.
source: Unexpectedly, however, 54% were heavily edited, many more than the 24% expected.
evidence: This is a comparison with the overall rate of heavy editing.

claim: Even in a background of hyper RNA editing, squid preferentially edit nervous system targets.
source: Thus even in a background of hyper RNA editing, squid, like other organisms, preferentially edit nervous system targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the enrichment of editing in nervous system genes.

claim: A squid ADAR2 ortholog can be expressed as two isoforms due to alternative splicing.
source: A past study showed that a squid ADAR2 ortholog can be expressed as two isoforms due to alternative splicing (Palavicini et al., 2009): one, having two double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding motifs, resembles vertebrate ADAR2s.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: One squid ADAR2 isoform, having two dsRNA binding motifs, resembles vertebrate ADAR2s.
source: A past study showed that a squid ADAR2 ortholog can be expressed as two isoforms due to alternative splicing (Palavicini et al., 2009): one, having two double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding motifs, resembles vertebrate ADAR2s.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: A second squid ADAR2 isoform contains an 'extra' dsRNA binding motif at its N-terminus.
source: A second, however, contains an 'extra' dsRNA binding motif at its N-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The non-canonical squid ADAR2 isoform edits RNA more efficiently.
source: This non-canonical isoform edits RNA more efficiently, edits more sites, and binds dsRNA with a far higher affinity (Palavicini et al., 2009, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The non-canonical squid ADAR2 isoform edits more sites.
source: This non-canonical isoform edits RNA more efficiently, edits more sites, and binds dsRNA with a far higher affinity (Palavicini et al., 2009, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The non-canonical squid ADAR2 isoform binds dsRNA with a far higher affinity.
